summary: The page closes the extended Chamber of the Lambs debate. Middot follows R. Eliezer ben Yaakov. Rav Adda b. R. Yitzchak explains that the Chamber of the Lambs extended along the west wall, appearing toward the south to one approaching from the north and toward the north to one approaching from the south. The Gemara then refines this view by placing it more toward the southwest and supports the perspective-based explanation through the parallel Tamid/Middot discrepancy about the showbread-preparation chamber, which Rav Huna b. Rav Yehoshua resolves by distinguishing rightward and leftward counting orders.

display.title: Closing the chamber debate through perspective and counting order
display.whats: The page identifies Middot with R. Eliezer ben Yaakov. Rav Adda bar R. Yitzchak then explains that the Chamber of the Lambs extended along the west wall, appearing toward the south to one approaching from the north and toward the north to one approaching from the south. The Gemara then refines the chamber's position toward the southwest and supports this perspective-based explanation with the parallel Tamid/Middot discrepancy about the showbread-preparation chamber.
display.hint: How can one chamber be described in different corners when each source counts the building from a different direction?

learning.learnerQuestion: How does Rav Adda's west-wall explanation reconcile the different corner descriptions of the Chamber of the Lambs?
learning.coreTension: Tamid and Middot appear to place the same chamber in different western corners.
learning.coreMove: Rav Adda places the chamber along the west wall, extending toward both corners, so its apparent corner depends on whether one approaches from the north or south. The Gemara refines its position toward the southwest and invokes the parallel discrepancy about the showbread-preparation chamber.
learning.resolution: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua explains the parallel discrepancy through counting direction: Middot counts by way of the right, while Tamid can be read as counting by way of the left. This bolsters the perspective-based account of the Chamber of the Lambs.

takeaway.text: Different corner descriptions can reflect approach and counting direction rather than different physical chambers.

learning.ahaMoment: The parallel showbread-chamber contradiction supplies the model: reverse the direction of counting, and the apparent north-south discrepancy disappears.
learning.learningBlocker: It is easy to read the corner names as fixed map coordinates without noticing that the sources enumerate the chambers from different directions.
learning.memoryAnchor: West-wall chamber, leaning southwest; north or south appearance follows the viewer's approach, just as right or left counting resolves the parallel chamber list.

argumentFlow.label: Verdict: Middot follows R. Eliezer ben Yaakov
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The weight of evidence establishes that Tractate Middot follows R. Eliezer ben Yaakov.

argumentFlow.label: Rav Adda: Chamber was on the middle of the west wall
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Adda bar R. Yitzchak
argumentFlow.text: Perhaps the Chamber of the Lambs was not in any corner at all but extended along the middle of the west wall. To one approaching from the north it appeared toward the south; to one approaching from the south it appeared toward the north.

argumentFlow.label: The chamber leaned southwest
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Chamber of the Lambs was positioned more toward the southwest. The Gemara supports this by noting a parallel disagreement: Tamid places the showbread-preparation chamber in the northeast, while Middot places it in the southeast.

sourceRefs.note: Southwest refinement and parallel chamber discrepancy

argumentFlow.label: Rav Huna: rightward and leftward counting
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
argumentFlow.text: Middot explicitly counts the chambers by way of the right, while Tamid can be understood as counting by way of the left. The reversed order resolves the apparent north-south discrepancy about the showbread-preparation chamber.

visualizableElements.item: Beit HaMoked with the Chamber of the Lambs along the west wall, leaning southwest, with arrows showing the north and south approaches
The four chambers listed clockwise and counterclockwise to show how north and south labels reverse

quizSeeds.question: How does Rav Adda explain the different corner descriptions of the Chamber of the Lambs?
quizSeeds.answer: The chamber extended along the west wall, so one approaching from the north saw it as toward the south, while one approaching from the south saw it as toward the north.

quizSeeds.question: How does Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua resolve the parallel discrepancy about the showbread-preparation chamber?
quizSeeds.answer: Middot counts the chambers by way of the right, while Tamid can be read as counting by way of the left, reversing the apparent north-south placement.

sugyot.finalRuling: Middot follows R. Eliezer ben Yaakov; Rav Adda's west-wall account is refined toward the southwest and supported by Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's right-versus-left counting resolution.
prerequisiteKnowledge: Tamid and Middot list the chambers in different orders

rashiTranslations.en: 'Rather, must you not conclude from this that it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view' - and it was obscured to him by the extra step, and not
because of the altar, since we hear Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov say, in the third chapter (below, 37a), that the entire
altar stands to the south, and the whole half of the entrance's open space is exposed. And if it should be asked: how
can the unattributed teaching of Middot be established according to his view, when we hear from this same unattributed teaching that the altar takes up
seven cubits to the north - necessarily,
this is how we must explain those twenty-five
cubits that you allot: that between the ramp
and the wall there are only five and a half cubits,
and the ramp and the altar sixty-two - so
the whole altar stands to the south, and all of it is opposite
the middle of the Courtyard, and the entire remainder goes to the place of
the nanasin. And if you say: if so, that the tanna was not precise
in dividing it into halves, and so you could increase
or decrease wherever you wish, then according to Rabbi Yehuda too you could
establish it, and the altar would be centered
in the middle of the Courtyard - how? Allot twenty-one
and a half of them between the ramp and the wall, and the ramp thirty, and half the altar's width sixteen -
it turns out the middle of the altar falls at sixty-seven and a half, which is the middle of the Courtyard! But this
you cannot say, that the place of the tables and the nanasin would be only three
and a half. And in my view it seems better to explain this teaching of Rav Adda bar Ahavah, and the whole passage,
in another way: Rav Adda bar Ahavah said 'whose view is this' regarding the mishna of Tamid,
'the appointed one said to them' - he stands on the fact that Middot is cast as contradicting the mishna of Tamid,
meaning that they dispute the unattributed teaching of Middot; it is Rabbi Yehuda's view, since we hear that he disputes the unattributed teaching
of Middot, for it is taught: Rabbi Yehuda says the altar is centered, etc. And if it should enter your mind that Middot is Rabbi Yehuda's view,
where would you find it? But we learned, etc., that shows the majority of the altar stands to the south - conclude from
this. And we do not read the phrase 'rather, must you not conclude from this that it is Rabbi Eliezer's view' as a fresh question; rather its meaning is: conclude from
this that Middot is not Rabbi Yehuda's view. 'Rav Adda bar Yitzchak said, this
chamber of the lambs juts out at its corners' - at its two corners it appears elongated,
standing in the west, and extending lengthwise to the north and south, close to the corners
on either side. 'And one coming from the north, it appears to him' - that it is drawn toward the south
more. 'And one coming from the south, it appears to him' - drawn toward the north. 'It stands to reason
that it was in the southwest' - more so; and the tanna of Tamid also agrees to this, except that he follows
the order from south to north, so it appears to him, in the way of his walking, as though it were
in the north. 'From the contradiction we raise regarding the showbread chamber' - for it was assumed that he counts
onward by way of the right, from north to west, and from west to south, and from south to east:
the chamber of the lambs in the northwest, the chamber of the seals in the
southwest, the chamber of the hearth in the southeast, the chamber of the showbread
in the northeast; and we would raise against this the mishna of Middot, which teaches that the southeast
corner - that was the chamber of the showbread. 'And we answer: Rav Huna
the son of Rav Yehoshua said' - the tanna of Middot counts by way of the right, as he explains
explicitly, that he goes and counts from south to east, and from east to north, and from north to west
and from west to south; and one who comes to circle around the whole building circles by way of the right,
from outside - this is the order of his circling; and as for the mishna of Tamid, which did not specify anything, one can
say that it counted by way of the left, and no further difficulty remains from now on
'If' - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment (granting that the tanna of Tamid himself agrees the chamber was toward the southwest) continues on 17b.
